primary_meaning: In Christian teaching the palm tree and palm branch most commonly symbolize victory and triumph — specifically the triumph of Christ (Palm Sunday) and, by extension, the victory of the righteous or of martyrs over sin, persecution, and death. Closely fused with this is the meaning of the flourishing, upright righteous person: 'The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree' (Psalm 92:12). Together these yield the standard composite: the palm represents the righteous who flourish and ultimately triumph.
primary_basis: Psalm 92:12-14 ('The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree')
John 12:13 (crowds take palm branches to greet Jesus at the triumphal entry)
Revelation 7:9 (the great multitude with palm branches before the throne, traditionally read as victorious saints/martyrs)
Leviticus 23:40 (palm fronds taken in rejoicing at the Feast of Tabernacles)
Song of Solomon 7:7-8 (stature 'like a palm tree')

alternatives.meaning: Righteous flourishing, uprightness, and fruitfulness in old age — the palm as an image of the godly person who stays green and productive (often treated as the primary meaning in Old Testament–focused teaching rather than an alternative).
Victory, triumph, and martyrdom — palm branches as emblems of conquest, taken up strongly in Christian art and liturgy (Palm Sunday; the palm of martyrdom in patristic and later tradition).
basis: 1 Maccabees 13:51 (extra-canonical, palm branches at Simon's victorious entry, often cited as background)

alternatives.meaning: Joy, festivity, and worship, connected to the Feast of Tabernacles and celebratory processions.
Temple, Eden/paradise, and the presence of God — palm carvings in Solomon's temple and Ezekiel's visionary temple read as restored-Eden imagery.
Life, refreshment, and provision in the wilderness — the palm as oasis tree (Elim; Jericho the 'city of palms').
Feminine beauty, stature, and grace (also reflected in Tamar as a woman's name).
Israel itself, or a specific covenant community, personified as the palm — found in some rabbinic midrash and occasional Christian typology.
basis: Judges 4:5 (the palm of Deborah, sometimes allegorized)

notes: The palm is one of the more stable biblical symbols. Two strands dominate and are usually blended: (1) the flourishing righteous (Psalm 92) and (2) victory/triumph (John 12; Revelation 7), the latter especially strong in Christian liturgy, iconography, and martyrology. There is no serious interpretive dispute over these core meanings; the alternatives listed are supplementary emphases rather than competing readings. The Hebrew word tamar also appears as a personal name (Genesis 38; 2 Samuel 13) and a place name (Tamar/Hazazon-tamar), which some studies fold into the symbolism but which mainstream interpretation treats separately.
